lead: Some problems have fast algorithms; some only have fast checks of a proposed answer. P names the first group and NP the second. The hardest problems in NP are NP-complete, and no polynomial-time algorithm is known for any of them. This chapter defines P, NP, reductions, NP-hardness and NP-completeness, states the Cook–Levin theorem, and shows the standard reduction chain. These ideas decide whether a problem is likely to have an efficient algorithm, so they matter in routing, scheduling, verification and competitive programming.
prereq: You need: 6.7 for TIME and SPACE classes and 6.2 for the idea of a reduction.

blocks.text: For a function t(n), TIME(t(n)) is the set of languages decided by a Turing machine that halts within t(n) steps on every input of length n. TIME(n^k) is the same class with t(n)=n^k. P is the union of TIME(n^k) over all constants k≥0. A language in P has a decider whose running time is polynomial in the input length. Sorting a list and testing whether a number is prime are standard examples; both have polynomial-time algorithms.

blocks.where: TIME(n^k) is the set of languages decided in O(n^k) time; n is the input length; the union ranges over every constant k.

blocks.text: NP is defined by certificates. A language L is in NP when there is a polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that for every string x: x ∈ L iff there exists a string y with |y| ≤ p(|x|) and V accepts the pair (x,y). The string y is a certificate or witness. V runs in time polynomial in |x|, so it cannot read more than polynomially many characters of y.

blocks.where: x is the input string; y is the certificate; p is a polynomial bound on certificate length; V is the polynomial-time verifier.

blocks.text: Equivalently, NP is the set of languages accepted by a polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machine: the machine guesses y and then runs V. A no-instance has no certificate, so no guess makes V accept. P ⊆ NP because a decider ignores the certificate and decides x directly. Nobody knows whether P = NP. The figure places P inside NP inside PSPACE.

A language A reduces to B in polynomial time, written A ≤p B, when some polynomial-time computable function f satisfies: for every x, x ∈ A iff f(x) ∈ B. The function f is the reduction. It maps yes-instances of A to yes-instances of B and no-instances to no-instances.
A ≤p B ⇔ ∃f computable in polynomial time, ∀x: x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B
blocks.where: A and B are languages; f is the reduction; x is any input string; ≤p is polynomial-time many-one reduction.

blocks.text: B is NP-hard when every language A in NP satisfies A ≤p B. B is NP-complete when B is NP-hard and B is also in NP. An NP-complete problem is therefore a hardest problem in NP: a polynomial-time decider for it would give a polynomial-time decider for every NP language.

To prove a new problem B is NP-complete, show B ∈ NP, then choose a known NP-complete A and prove A ≤p B. The direction matters: reducing B to A proves nothing about B's hardness. NP-hard is a lower-bound label; it does not require membership in NP. Some NP-hard problems are undecidable and hence outside NP.

Cook–Levin theorem: SAT is NP-complete. SAT asks whether a Boolean formula in variables x1,...,xn has an assignment making it true. The proof encodes the computation of a polynomial-time nondeterministic machine as a Boolean formula whose satisfying assignments correspond to accepting computation paths. 3SAT, the restriction to clauses of exactly three literals, is also NP-complete.

Standard reductions give SAT ≤p 3SAT ≤p CLIQUE ≤p VERTEX-COVER. CLIQUE asks whether a graph has a set of k vertices all pairwise adjacent. VERTEX-COVER asks whether a graph has a set of k vertices touching every edge. SUBSET-SUM asks whether some subset of a given set of integers adds to a target T. HAMILTONIAN CYCLE asks whether a graph has a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once. All are NP-complete.

Whether P = NP is open. If any NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, then P = NP, because every NP language reduces to it. Most researchers believe P ≠ NP, but no proof exists. co-NP contains languages whose complements are in NP; for example, unsatisfiability of Boolean formulas is in co-NP. NP and co-NP are both contained in PSPACE, the languages decided with polynomial tape. TQBF, the true quantified Boolean formula problem, is PSPACE-complete.

figure.caption: The arrows trace the certificate 1,2,3,4,5 on the worked example's graph, so the verifier's five edge lookups are 12, 23, 34, 45 and the closing edge 51 — all present. Ten pairwise comparisons confirm the five vertices are distinct, so the check costs O(n²) time, which is what puts HAMILTONIAN CYCLE in NP.

spec.aria: A graph on vertices 1 to 5 with the certificate cycle drawn as arrows 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 to 5 back to 1, plus two dashed extra edges 13 and 24.

examples.question: Show that HAMILTONIAN CYCLE is in NP, using the graph G on vertices 1 to 5 with edges 12, 23, 34, 45, 51, 13 and 24. Use the cycle certificate 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Count the verifier's edge lookups and comparisons, and give the order of its running time.
steps: A yes-instance must carry a certificate. Here the certificate y is the sequence of vertices (1,2,3,4,5).
The verifier checks that the 5 vertices are distinct. It compares the sequence entries and finds no repeat, so this check passes.
It checks the four consecutive edges 12, 23, 34, 45. All four are present in G, so these lookups pass.
It checks that edge 51 closes the cycle. That edge is present, so the closure check passes.

Count the work: the verifier makes 5 edge lookups (four consecutive edges plus the closing edge) and up to 10 pairwise comparisons to confirm the 5 vertices are distinct. For n=5, n²=25 and 15 ≤ 25, so the work is of order n², a polynomial (in general n edge lookups and n(n-1)/2 comparisons).
examples.answer: The certificate is checked with 5 edge lookups and 10 comparisons, which is within O(n²) time for n=5, so HAMILTONIAN CYCLE is in NP. The problem is also NP-complete, so a polynomial-time decider for it would prove P = NP.
examples.check:
edges = {frozenset((1,2)), frozenset((2,3)), frozenset((3,4)), frozenset((4,5)), frozenset((5,1)), frozenset((1,3)), frozenset((2,4))}
cycle = [1,2,3,4,5]
n = len(cycle)
assert len(set(cycle)) == n
pairs = [(cycle[i], cycle[(i+1) % n]) for i in range(n)]
assert all(frozenset(p) in edges for p in pairs)
edge_lookups = len(pairs)
comparisons = n*(n-1)//2
print(edge_lookups)
print(comparisons)
print(n*n)

traps: NP does not mean 'not polynomial'. It means nondeterministic polynomial time, equivalently a polynomial-time checkable certificate for yes-instances.
NP-hard problems need not be in NP; NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP.
To prove B NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem A to B (A ≤p B), not B to A.
Certificates exist only for yes-instances. A no-instance of an NP language has no accepted certificate; a verifier may reject every short string.
P = NP is open. A fast algorithm for one NP-complete problem would settle it, but none is known.

quiz.q: Define the class P and state the union formula.
quiz.a: P = ∪ TIME(n^k) over all constants k≥0; TIME(n^k) holds languages decided by a Turing machine in O(n^k) time.
SAT is NP-complete; hence 3SAT is NP-complete by reduction from SAT.
A polynomial-time decider ignores the certificate and decides x directly, so every P language has a polynomial-time verifier.

quiz.q: What is a certificate for a yes-instance of SAT?
quiz.a: A truth assignment to the variables that makes the formula true; the verifier checks every clause.

quiz.q: For the graph in the worked example, certificate (1,2,3,4,5): list the five edge lookups and say whether they all succeed.
quiz.a: Edges 12, 23, 34, 45, 51. All exist in G, so the certificate is accepted.

quiz.q: If A ≤p B and A is NP-complete, what do you know about B?
quiz.a: B is NP-hard. If B is also in NP, then B is NP-complete; otherwise B is only NP-hard.

quiz.q: Why does proving B ≤p SAT not show B is NP-hard?
quiz.a: The reduction direction is wrong. NP-hardness of B needs every NP language, including SAT, to reduce to B, i.e. SAT ≤p B.

quiz.q: Explain why a polynomial-time algorithm for CLIQUE would settle P = NP.
quiz.a: CLIQUE is NP-complete, so every NP language reduces to it. A polynomial-time decider for CLIQUE would decide every NP language in polynomial time, giving P = NP.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern SAT solvers decide many industrial instances despite SAT being NP-complete, and hardware and software verification relies on them. Approximation algorithms and parameterized complexity look for useful answers when exact polynomial-time algorithms are unlikely. Cryptography uses the assumed hardness of problems such as factoring, which is not known to be NP-complete. Search terms: SAT solver, NP-hard scheduling, approximation ratio, parameterized complexity, co-NP.
